plate_findings.evidence: T2 sagittal spine MRI showing symmetric T2 hypersignal in the anterior horns of the spinal cord (Figure 1; in-text: 'areas with symmetrical T2 hypersignals bilaterally in the anterior horns of the spinal cord')

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Sagittal T2-weighted spinal MRI of a 5-year-old boy with a polio-like acute flaccid syndrome showing the longitudinally extensive anterior horn T2 signal abnormality; genuine untreated patient imaging consistent with poliomyelitis anterior horn involvement. B: Axial T2 spinal MRI demonstrating the classic bilateral symmetric anterior horn 'snake eye' hyperintensity (arrows) in a polio-like acute flaccid syndrome; hallmark MRI manifestation of poliomyelitis.
panels.attribution_text: Pereira et al. Acute flaccid myelitis in a polio-like syndrome.. Revista da Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina Tropical 2020. doi:10.1590/0037-8682-0259-2020. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1:.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine, T2 sagittal (A) and T2 axial (B). Bilaterally symmetric circular to ovoid foci of high T2-weighted signals in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord compatible with the “snake eye” sign (arrows in B).
in_text_mentions: A previously healthy 5-year-old boy was admitted for fever, vomiting, and dyspnea, evolving with masticatory automatism, areflexia, and asymmetric flaccid tetraparesis, with preserved sensitivity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine showed areas with symmetrical T2 hypersignals bilaterally in the anterior horns of the spinal cord, without contrast enhancement, in a “snake eye” sign (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: Axial T1-weighted MRI shows asymmetric amyotrophy and marked fatty replacement

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 10 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J). A: Axial T1 panel in post-polio syndrome article showing asymmetric amyotrophy/fatty replacement, matching post-polio limb atrophy. B: T1 axial thigh showing asymmetric amyotrophy/fatty replacement attributed to Post-Poliomyelitis Syndrome. C: T1 axial thigh with asymmetric fatty replacement in PPS case. D: T1 axial lower-leg panels showing amyotrophy/fatty replacement of tibialis anterior/gastrocnemius in PPS. E: T1 axial lower-leg showing amyotrophy/fatty replacement in PPS patient. F: STIR axial showing acute-on-chronic denervation hyperintensity in same PPS limbs with amyotrophy; atrophy present visually, hyperintensity proposed. G: STIR axial denervation hyperintensity in PPS thigh muscles. H: Coronal T1 showing asymmetric amyotrophy/fatty replacement in PPS. I: Coronal STIR showing denervation change in PPS lower limbs with underlying atrophy. J: Full-leg coronal STIR showing PPS denervation/amyotrophy pattern.
panels.attribution_text: Braga et al. Segmental areas of denervation in post-polio syndrome.. Arquivos de neuro-psiquiatria 2024. doi:10.1055/s-0044-1779507. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Muscle MRI studies. Axial ( A-E ) and coronal ( H ) T1-weighted MRI shows asymmetric amyotrophy and marked fatty replacement involving bilateral vastus lateralis, right vastus intermedius, left biceps femoris, right vastus medialis, left tibialis anterior, and bilateral heads of gastrocnemius. Axial ( F,G ) and coronal ( I,J ) STIR MRI shows hyperintensity involving right vastus lateralis and tibialis anterior.
in_text_mentions: Electromyography disclosed bilateral chronic lumbosacral denervation and mild acute denervation involving the right lower limb. Neuroimaging studies (brain and spinal MRI) and genetic testing (MLPA test for quantification of SMN1 and SMN2 copy numbers and hereditary neuropathy, non-5q, and other motor neuron disease panels) were normal. Muscle MRI disclosed asymmetric neurogenic muscle “islands” alternating areas with and without fatty replacement ( Figure 1 ), 1 suggestive of Post-Poliomyelitis Syndrome (PPS). 2 3 Muscle MRI is useful to distinguish PPS from other motor neuron diseases. 1 2 3

in_text_mentions: had no trauma history. Currently, the patient presented with progressive pain and limited range in both knees. On physical examination, the patient has bilateral valgus and bilateral knee recurvatum of 40°, a shortening of 3 cm of the left lower limb (Figure 1). The quadriceps force of both knees was 3/5. The left knee range of motion (ROM) was 40-0º-60º, while the right knee ROM was 40º-0-80º. Both knees had global laxity (anteroposterior and mediolateral), with more severe on the left side. The patient has a valgus flat foot, more marked on the left. The examination of both hips was normal.

panels.rationale: H&E histopathology of the gluteus medius muscle from a polio survivor showing diffuse fat infiltration with scattered atrophic muscle fibers and no acute inflammation or atypia. The article title ('Unusual MRI Findings in a Polio Survivor') and in-text mention explicitly attribute the specimen changes to the involved muscle in poliomyelitis, supporting disease attribution. The histologic pattern of fatty replacement with atrophic fibers is a classic post-polio muscle manifestation. No vocabulary key directly describes muscle fatty infiltration/atrophy (the histology key refers to anterior horn motor neuron loss), so the histologic findings are recorded as proposed findings.

in_text_mentions: nce phase of gait occurs when the quadriceps power is less than Grade II on the MRC scale. Children with Grade III power may walk well on an even surface on level ground but often experience instability while walking on uneven ground or while negotiating slopes or stairs. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Sagittal knee MRI of a confirmed polio patient (article title: 'polyethylene tibial fracture in a polio patient'). The joint itself was reported as unremarkable/no abnormalities, but the surrounding musculature shows markedly reduced bulk with fatty replacement consistent with post-polio limb atrophy, a recognized polio manifestation visible on imaging. B: Second sagittal MRI cut of the same polio patient's knee; muscle compartments around the joint appear thin with fatty infiltration, supporting post-polio limb muscle atrophy. Caption itself reports no joint abnormalities, so disease attribution rests on the visible atrophic musculature rather than a captioned finding.
